Narendra Nath Basu Roy and another ------ Appellant.
 Vs.
Municipal Committee Mymensingh ------ Respondents.
full_judgment: 13. It is undeniable fact that the land vested in the Municipality since 1932 and therefore, the defendant were only tenants of the land belonging to the Municipality by taking a temporary lease for nine years which however was renewed from time to time. The teamed Courts below unfortunately did not approach the facts of the case from the correct legal aspect. The High Court Division repelled the contention that after the wholesale acquisition by the Government the defendant has become a tenant under the Government and that the Maharaja has lost his paramount interest. This contention was repelled by the High Court Division by saying "the plaintiff is very much the owner of the suit land and cannot be denied any relief in the suit on the ground that it has lost its title," Mr. Pal argued that the question was not answered in the judgments of the courts below as to how this suit land vested in the Municipality and how it is exonerated from the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The answer is what we have given already that by the general notification affecting the rent receiving interest and the khas land of the rent receiver, the land which has vested with the Municipality since 1932 was not affected and therefore, the contentious of the defendants do not hold good, And. secondly the defendants' plea of adverse possession, as noticed already, has no substance. The trial court found that the defendants had constructed pucca structures in violation of the terms of the kabuliyat and these structures were raised some 20/25 years back. The view was taken that their possession "was adverse to the knowledge of Municipality' and in these circumstances "the Municipality was with the right of collecting cent and tax only as in the meantime the defendant 1 and his brother acquired tenancy right by adverse possession." The appellate court below though affirmed the judgment and order of the trial court took the view that the questions of adverse possession does not arise in this case and concluded that Sailendra continued to be a tenant by holding over.
